caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 4057 of 2018.
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Attorney-General, instructed by Haridas Paul, Advocate-on-Record-----For the Petitioner. 
AJ Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Tawfique Hossain, Advocate-on-Record-----For the Respondents.
parties:
Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh and others-------Petitioners 
Vs 
Md Mushfaqur Rahman and another-------Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 16-7-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 631 of 2010).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain CJ: This civil petition for leave to appeal is direction against the judgment and order dated 16-7-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 631 of 2010 making the Rule Nisi absolute.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this civil petition for leave to appeal, in brief, are:

The writ-petitioners are law abiding citizens and come from respectable Muslim families. One Mr Ahsan Habib applied to the Government for allotment of Khas land within Cox's Bazar's Hotel/Motel Zone for construction of a hotel. The Government allotted 1.00 acre of land initially but the land was submerged in water. Subsequently, the Government allotted Plot No. 13 (Kolatoli Road) on 26-1-2003 by a lease deed for a period of 99 years. Thereafter, the lessee Mr Habib filed an application before the Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar seeking permission to transfer the allotted land in favour of the writ-petitioners. The application was allowed and the writ-petitioners deposited transfer fees on 13-7-2006. Thereafter, on 27-6-2006 transfer deed had been executed and registered. The writ-petitioners thereafter mutated the land in their names. After that, the writ-petitioners obtained possession of the land and constructed boundary walls and proceeded with the construction work. The writ-petitioners, in one part of the land constructed a Motel which was rented out to the tourists. Soon thereafter, the Care-taker Government took over charge. As a result, due to unavoidable circumstances, the construction work had to be suspended temporarily.

3. In 2009, the writ-petitioners obtained No Objection Certificate' from the Civil Aviation Authority for the construction of the hotel. The writ-petitioners also prepared plan and submitted the same to the Paurashova and the plan was approved on 19-6-2009. On 01-7-2009, they submitted a copy of the approved plan to the Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar. The writ-petitioners also filed applications to the Deputy Commissioner, Cox's Bazar and the Ministry of Land seeking three years extension for completion of the project. However, no decision on the applications had been communicated to the writ-petitioners. Thereafter, writ-respondent No. 2 abruptly issued the order dated 12-1-2010 (impugned before the High Court Division) informing the writ-petitioners that the lease agreement had been cancelled and directed the writ-petitioners to hand-over the land to the Government. Prior to the cancellation of lease no show cause notice had been issued.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with order dated 12-1-2010 issued under the signature of writ-respondent No. 2, the writ-petitioners moved the High Court Division by filing a writ petition and obtained Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 631 of 2010.

5. Writ-respondent No.1 filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the material statements made in the writ petition. It was stated that the order dated 12-1-2020 was issued in the light of a detailed inspection report and therefore, there was no illegality in issuing the impugned order. It was also pointed out that prior to issuance of the cancellation order, an inter-ministerial meeting was held on 28-5-2009. A committee was formed in the said meeting and the representatives of the Committee visited Cox's Bazar and found that the writ-petitioners and others violated the terms of lease agreement. This led to the issuance of the lever of cancellation. Writ-respondent No. 1 also relied on certain judgments passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 639, 511 and 894 of 2010 in support of their contention and, as such, the Rule should be discharged.

6. A supplementary affidavit-in-opposition had also been filed. It was stated therein that the lease agreement was cancelled on 12-1-2010 and subsequently, the writ-respondents obtained possession of the land in question.

7. The writ-petitioners filed a supplementary-affidavit from which it appears that a list of 59 plots was prepared showing breach of terms of the lease deed and it was recommended that lease in respect of those plots should be cancelled. It was pointed out, amongst others, that in preparing the list no show cause notice was issued. By another supplementary-affidavit, the writ-petitioners have annexed a letter dated 26-8-2015 which shows that the writ-petitioners' plot is not within the ecologically critical area.

8. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties by the judgment and order dated 16-7-2017 made the Rule absolute.

9. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the writ-respondents as the leave-petitioners filed this civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

10. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the leave-petitioners, submits that the original lessee Md Ahsan Habib seriously violated the mandatory conditions of lease-agreement (Annexure-B to the writ petition) and that because of violation of mandatory condition of lease agreement, the cancellation order dated 12-1-2010 passed by the Government is quite legal and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. He further submits that both the plots in question are situated within Jhilanja Mouza which is within the Ecologically Critical Area (ECA) and is protected by the prohibitions mentioned in the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 and, as such, leasing out those plots were illegal and without jurisdiction. He then submits that by the subsequent Notification dated 3-5-1999 only the reserve forest areas are excluded from the ECA, and not the sea beach area. He then submits that the subsequent letter dated 2-11-2015 issued by the Department of Environment was somehow procured after the judgment was delivered by the High Court Division arising out of similar writ petitions. He also submits that the aforesaid letter dated 2-11-2015 was issued at the instance of one of the parties and it cannot override the Notification dated 19-4-1999 published in the official Gazette.

11. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the subsequent purchasers from the original lessee, submits that the impugned order of cancellation was issued in violation of principle of natural justice as no prior notice was served upon them before cancellation of the lease agreement. He also submits that respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the subsequent purchasers from the original lessee relied upon the letter issued by the appropriate authority approving the transfer and that the writ-petitioners paid the transfer fees which. were accepted by the proper authority and the names of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein were mutated and, as such, the impugned order of cancellation is illegal and without lawful authority. He then submits that the disputed plots were not within ECA as evident from Annexure-M dated 26-8-2015 signed by Assistant Director, Paribesh Directorate, Cox's Bazar and, as such, the impugned cancellation of lease was illegal and without jurisdiction. He lastly submits that the present case is distinguishable from writ petitions disposed of by the High Court Division vide judgment and order dated 22-7-2010 and, as such, the impugned judgment and order calls for no interference.

12. One Mohammad Ahsan Habib applied to the Government for allotment of khas land within Cox's Bazar Hotel/Motel Zone for construction of a Hotel. The Government allotted 1 (one) acre of land initially but the land was submerged in water. Later the Government allotted plot No.13 (Kolatoli Road) on 26-1-2003. The lessee filed an application before the Deputy Commissioner, Cox's Bazar, seeking permission to transfer the allotted land in favour of the writ-petitioners. The application was allowed and the writ-petitioners deposited transfer fees on 13-7-2006. After that, the transfer deed was executed and registered on 27-6-2006. In 2009, the writ petitioners obtained No objection Certificate from Civil Aviation Authority for construction of the hotel. The writ-petitioners also prepared plan and submitted the same with the Paurashova which approved it on 19-6-2006. They filed applications to the Deputy Commissioner, Cox's Bazar and the Ministry of Land seeking 3 years extension for completion of the project. But no decision on those applications had been communicated to the petitioners. After that, writ-respondent No. 2 abruptly issued the order dated 12-1-2010 (impugned before the High Court Division) informing the writ-petitioners that the lease agreement has been cancelled and directed the writ-petitioners to hand over the land to the Government.

13. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that the impugned order was issued arbitrarily, not taking into account the relevant facts and that the High Court Division was convinced that the impugned order was issued in violation of the principle of natural justice. The High Court Division found that a lease agreement was not automatically nullified and that it had to be nullified. The High Court Division noticed that since the lease agreement was not cancelled prior to the transfer approval in favour of the writ-petitioners, a right under a valid lease was transferred in favour of the writ-petitioners. The High Court Division noted that admittedly the writ-petitioners could not complete the work within the period of 3 years but that on its own could not justify the order of cancellation of lease dated 12-1-2010. The High Court Division found that the impugned decision to cancel lease was taken on the recommendation of a committee which recommended that 59 plots should be cancelled including the plots belonging to the writ-petitioners. The High Court Division then held there was nothing on record that the committee heard the lessees including the writ petitioners prior to the recommendation for cancellation and that the order of cancellation based on committee's recommendation was illegal.

14. With regard to the claim of illegal cancellation of the lease, we find from the papers submitted by the writ-respondents that the lease was cancelled as both the plots were found empty, that is, there was no construction. Therefore, the writ-petitioners were in breach of the terms and conditions specified in the lease deed.

15. The learned Attorney-General mainly concentrated his argument on the preservation of ecological balance of the environment and protection of natural resources. The learned Attorney-General submits that the Government granted the lease without taking notice of the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 declaring Cox's Bazar Sea Beach as Ecologically Critical Area (ECA) under section 5 of the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995.

16. The learned Counsel for the writ-petitioner-respondents draws attention to the second Gazette Notification dated 3-5-1999 by which the disputed two plots were excluded from ECA. With regard to the submission that both the plots have been excluded in the later Gazette Notification dated 3-5-1999, the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 22-7-2010 delivered in Writ Petition No.639 of 2010 and others held as follows:

"We have meticulously examined the notification dated 3-5-1999 by which certain areas were excluded from the declaration and found that “কক্সবাজার জেলার কক্সবাজার-টেকনাফ সমুদ্র সৈকত ও সোনাদিয়া দ্বীপ এর সংশ্লিষ্ট রিজার্ভ ফরেস্ট এলাকাসমূহ, বর্ণিত প্রজ্ঞাপন উল্লিখিত বিধি নিষেধের আওতা বহির্ভূত করা হলো।” Thus this clearly means that রিজার্ভ ফরেস্ট এলাকাসমূহ, বর্ণিত প্রজ্ঞাপনে উল্লিখিত বিধি নিষেধের আওতা বহির্ভূত করা হলো।This means "Reserved Forest Area" of the Cox's Bazar Sea Beach has been excluded from the Ecologically Critical Area but not the Cox' s Bazar Sea Beach from the declaration of Ecologically Critical Area."

17. We have considered the schedule of the lease deed dated 26-1-2003 as contained in Annexure-B to the writ petition and found that only the land of Jhilanja Mouza was included in the schedule of the lease deed. The schedule is quoted below:

23. This letter was issued at the instance of Md K Rahman alias Md Katikbur Rahman, the constituted attorney of both the writ petitioners. Before issuance of the letter dated 26-8-2015, the High Court Division delivered its judgment in other writ petitions on 22-7-2010. But a letter cannot override the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 which included all the areas of Mouza, namely, Jhilanja. In that Notification, no exception has been made on the basis of category of land. The Notification dated 19-4-1999 has simply included all lands within Jhilanja Mouza as ECA. Therefore, we are of the view that the letter dated 26-8-2015 is misconceived and contravenes the official Gazette. The said letter is, therefore, of no legal effect.

24. In addition to above, the said letter dated 26-8-2015 was signed by the Assistant Director, Paribesh Directorate, Cox's Bazar. In the affidavit-in-opposition dated 9-7-2017, it has been stated the officer who had signed the letter dated 26-8-2015 was not authorized to issue such letter and that no report was called for from him by any Court or Ministry of Land. The Assistant Director, Paribesh Directorate, Cox's Bazar, had issued the letter without any direction from proper authority and it was issued with ill motive.

25. This Division in the case of Farid Ahmed Chowdhury and another vs Ministry of Land, represented by its Secretary, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others delivered the judgment and order dated 09-12-2018 in Civil Review Petition Nos. 305-306 of 2015 with Civil" Review Petition Nos. 315-316 of 2015 and Civil Review Petition No. 320 of 2015 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2367 of 2010 and held that the plots in question are not excluded from ECA. The exclusions of the writ-petitioners' plots from the ECA being the main thrust of their submissions, we do not find any merit in these review petitions. Therefore, in those cases, this Division directed as under:

"All leases within Jhilanja Mouza granted after 19-4-1999 be cancelled in the same way as those of the writ-petitioners and any constructions made thereon be demolished. Of course, the lease holder shall be compensated for their loss due to such cancellation/demolition. We further direct that henceforth no lease shall be granted within Jhiianja Mouza or any area which has been classified as Ecologically Critical Area (ECA)."

26. The Ecologically Critical Area (ECA) is an environmentally protected zone where the ecosystem is considered to be endangered to reach a critical condition by the changes brought through various human activities. Section 2(gg) of the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995 as amended till date provides that "Ecologically critical Area" means such area which is rich in unique bio-diversity or due to the importance of environmental perspective necessary to protect or conserve from destructive activities. ECA also falls within the category of natural and cultural heritage.

27. The Government of Bangladesh has declared eight areas as ECAs in 1999, e.g. Cox's Bazar and Teknaf Peninsula, St. Martin's Island, Sonadia Island, Hakaluki Haor, Tanguar Haor and Marjat Baor, Gulshan-Baridhara Lake and Sundarbans. Subsequently in 2009, four rivers (e.g. Buriganga, Sitalakhya, Balu and Turag) around. Dhaka city were declared as ECAs.

28. Bangladesh is a signatory to the Ramsar Convention (1971) and the World Heritage Convention (1972) which are the principal instruments ensuring the conservation of natural heritages worldwide. The principal legislations that safeguard ECAs in Bangladesh are the Environment Conservation Act (1995), Environment Conservation Rules (1997), and the Constitution of Bangladesh.

29. The Act of 1995 in its section 5(1) contains provisions regarding declaration of ECA by the DG of the Department of Environment (DoE), which provides that if the Government is satisfied that, an area is in an environmentally critical situation or is threatened to be in such situation, the Government may declare such area as an ECA. Sub-section (2) also points out that, the Government shall under sub-section (1), specify the activities or processes that cannot be initiated or continued in an ECA. The Act also confers power to DoE to order corrective steps to be taken by any person believed to be responsible directly or indirectly, for causing harm to the ecosystem. Again, Rule 3(1) of the Rules of 1997 states that, the Government shall take the following factors into consideration while declaring any area as ECA under section 5(1) of the Act: (a) human habitat;(b) ancient monument; (c) archeological site; (d) forest sanctuary; (e) national park; (f) game reserve; (g) wild animals habitat; (h) wetland; (i) mangrove; (j) forest area; (k) bio-diversity of the relevant area; and (1) Other relevant factors. Furthermore, Article 18A of the Bangladesh Constitution contains provisions regarding the protection and improvement of environment and bio-diversity and states that, the State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to preserve and safeguard the natural resources, bio-diversity, wetlands, forests and wild life for the present and future citizens.

30. Therefore, the lease deed dated 26-1-2003 in favour of Ahsan Habib, the vendor of the writ-petitioners, for construction of hotel, was illegal from its very inception in view of Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 made under section 5 of the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995.

31. In addition to above, the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act has a non obstante in section 2A of the Act, which runs as follows:

"Overriding effect of the Act—Notwithstanding anything contained to the contrary in any other law for the time being in force, the provisions of this Act, rules and directions issued under this Act shall have effect."

32. Therefore, it appears that the provisions of this law shall prevail over any other law for the time being in force and, as such, no derogatory act can be done in violation of the Gazette Notification dated 19-4-1999 made under section 5 of the Environment Conservation Act, 1995 as amended till date.

33. In spite of legal prohibitions, the Metro Makers and Developers Limited (MMDL), a private company, undertook a development project and started earth-filling in the project area which was earmarked as Sub-Flood Flow Zone (SFFZ). In such a situation, the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers' Association (BELA), which is an organization of the environmental activist-lawyers, made a survey visiting the project area and felt the necessity of stopping such illegal works against environmental protection. The said group of lawyers (BELA) ultimately brought the matter before the Supreme Court for adjudication. Giving its decision reported in 65 DLR (AD) 181, the Appellate Division held that the right to-life as guaranteed by the Constitution includes the right to protection and improvement of the environment and ecology and, therefore, the said project of Metro Makers and Developers Limited was declared unlawful. The Court further directed the Metro Makers to restore the wetland of that area to its original state.

34. In the recent past, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, on umpteen occasions, has given directives and guidelines to the government to demarcate the rivers as per their original borderlines and to restore free flow of water restraining the illegal attempts of their enforcements and to save them from being perished. Many housing companies and land developers found engaged in changing the nature and features of wetlands and rivers have already been stopped because of the proactive role of the Judiciary of Bangladesh. But, nevertheless, we have a long way to go and take a firm stand to build up public awareness and legislate more stringent laws to cope with the needs of the changing society, otherwise it will be difficult for us to protect the bountiful treasures of nature and ensure environmental security without which the lives of our posterity will be at stake.

35. Public Interest Litigation under Article 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India resulted in a wave of environmental litigations. The leading environmental cases decided by the Supreme Court includes case of closure of limestone quarries in the Dehradun region (Dehradun Quarrying case. Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra, Dehrandun vs State of UP, AIR 1985 SC 652), the installation of safeguard at a chlorine plant in Delhi (MC Mehta vs Union of India, AIR 1988 SC 1037) etc. in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum vs Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647, the Court observed that "the Precautionary Principle" and "the Polluter Pays Principle" are essential features of "Sustainable Development."

36. At local and village level also, Panchayats have been empowered under the Constitution of India to take measures such as soil conservation, water management, forestry and protection of the environment and promotion of ecological aspect.

37. Environment protection is a part of Indian cultural values and traditions. In Atharvaveda (knowledge), it has been said that "Man's paradise is on earth; this living world is the beloved place of all; It has the blessings of nature's bounties; live in a lovely spirit". Earth is our paradise and it is our duty to protect our paradise. The constitution of India embodies the framework of protection and preservation of nature without which life cannot be enjoyed. The knowledge of constitutional provisions regarding environment protection is need of the day to bring greater public participation, environmental awareness, environmental education and sensitize the people to preserve ecology environment.

38. In order to successfully confront the twenty-first century environmental challenges that include managing the current and mitigating the future impacts of climate change; conserving natural resources and bio-diversity and preventing pollution, and to ensure environmental justice, it is incumbent upon the state to develop, implement and enforce environmental laws and upon the Judiciary to see that all parties concerned follow the laws and no one transgresses the same.

39. 19th century Native American leader Chief Seattle said,

"We do not inherit the Earth from our ancestors. We borrowed it from our Children"

40. We will have to return this Earth to our descendants so that they can return it to their future generations.

41. In the light of the findings made above, we find substance in this civil petition for leave to appeal. Accordingly, this civil petition is disposed of and the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division is set aside.

Respondent No.1 is directed to return the consideration money mentioned in the lease deed to both the writ-petitioners if they approach the Secretary, Ministry of Land.
